opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most interesting tensions in AI products right now. Historically, the internet's big winners usually started very focused. You find one use case, do it extremely well, and then expand. Search started with search. Social started with a specific campus or community. With general AI agents, it's tempting to say, "the model can do everything, so let's build a product that does everything." But users don't come to a product for "everything." They come because they have a specific problem today.

So the way I'd frame it is this: the **capability** can be general, but the **entry point** has to be specific. You need a few anchor use cases where the product is clearly, almost unfairly, better than the alternatives, whether that's research, data analysis, writing slides, or coding. Those are what people tell their friends about, and that's what builds the habit. Once people trust it for one thing, they naturally start trying it for adjacent things. That's where the general form actually pays off, because you don't need to build a new product for every new use case.

There's also a technical reason to keep the general form. If you over-specialize, you end up building lots of hand-crafted workflows and scaffolding. That might work well for six months, but then the next model comes out and a lot of that engineering becomes unnecessary, or even gets in the way. That's the bitter lesson again. A general architecture lets you ride the improvement of the underlying models instead of fighting it.

But the risk of being too general is that you become a demo. People are impressed, try it a few times, and don't come back, because nothing in their daily life depends on it. So I think the right balance looks something like this:

- **Keep the agent core general.** Give it tools, an environment, memory, and the ability to take long-horizon actions, and don't hard-code too much.
- **Make the product surface opinionated.** Choose a few scenarios, polish them deeply, and measure whether people actually finish real tasks and return.
- **Let usage data decide expansion.** Watch what people try to do that you didn't design for. That's the signal for the next focused application.

And honestly, I think the deeper question is about the **utility**, not the product form. What's the real value the user gets, and is it getting better over time? If the general product keeps compounding through memory, context about the user, and better models, then generality becomes a moat. If it doesn't, then a focused vertical product with deep context in one domain will probably win in that domain.

So my short answer: be general underneath and specific on top, and stay honest about which use cases people actually love.

r001.rationale: It says the agent core can remain general while the product surface focuses on a few specific, polished use cases.

r002.rationale: It says a general product can support adjacent use cases without building a new product for each, but does not state that this gives it a higher ceiling than a product confined to one domain.

r003.rationale: It explains that anchor use cases build habit and trust, after which users try adjacent uses and usage data guides expansion to the next focused application.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the tension you're describing is real, but I'd frame it a little differently. A general-purpose product and a focused application aren't two ends of a spectrum you pick a point on. They're two layers, and the question is really about how they talk to each other.

The broad form, the chat interface, the agent that can take arbitrary instructions, that's where you discover what people actually want. You can't predict it in advance. When we built things like ReAct or SWE-agent, the interesting use cases were never the ones we designed for. People showed up and did things with it that surprised us, and those surprises were the signal. So the general product is partly a research instrument. It's how you learn the distribution of real demand.

But a general interface is also a bad product for most specific jobs. If someone wants to debug a codebase, or fill out a tax form, or manage their calendar, telling them "here's a blank box, describe what you want" is pushing a lot of cognitive load onto the user. The focused application is where you take what you learned from the broad layer and you compress it. You build the scaffolding, the tools, the memory, the UI affordances, so the user doesn't have to re-explain the context every time. That's where the value gets captured.

So my view for something like Midas is: keep the general form as the top of the funnel and as the place you watch. Then be very disciplined about which focused applications you actually build. The failure mode I worry about is trying to be a little bit good at everything. Agents are only as useful as their environment lets them be. If you give the model a weak environment for a hundred tasks, it looks mediocre at all of them. If you give it a really well-designed environment for three tasks, it looks like magic on those three, and that's what people remember.

The other thing I'd say is that the boundary moves. Three years ago, coding needed a very specialized product. Now the base model is strong enough that a lot of that specialization is less necessary, and the general agent can handle it with lighter scaffolding. So whatever focused applications you build today, you should expect some of them to get absorbed back into the general layer. That's fine. That's actually the sign that the whole thing is working. The focused apps are a bet on where the model isn't yet, and you should be willing to retire them as the model catches up.

r001.rationale: The response says the general-purpose product and focused applications are compatible layers, with focused apps built from what is learned through the broad interface.

r002.rationale: It describes the general interface as handling arbitrary instructions and surfacing unexpected use cases, in contrast to focused apps designed for particular jobs. This communicates a broader potential application range.

r003.rationale: The response discusses learning from broad use and building or retiring focused apps as models improve, but does not say that killer applications at successive stages sustain the general-purpose product’s growth.

astra-6.text:
I think you can have a general-purpose product, but you still need a very specific reason for someone to use it. Those are two different questions: what the system can do, and where it delivers enough value that people come back.

For a product like Midas, I would start with a few applications where you can understand the user’s goal and judge whether the task was actually completed. If the application is too broad from the beginning, it becomes difficult to tell whether you’re improving the product or just adding more things it can demonstrate.

At the same time, you want to be careful about building each application as a completely separate system. Ideally, the capabilities you develop for one task—using tools, keeping track of context, recovering from mistakes—also help with other tasks. Then focused applications become a way to develop and test the general capability.

So I would keep the product’s ambition broad, but make the initial user promise concrete. Earn trust by doing something useful reliably, and expand as the system becomes capable of taking on more.

r001.rationale: It says a general-purpose product can start with a few focused applications, making broad capability and focused use cases compatible.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the potential application ceiling of a general-purpose product with a domain-confined product such as an IDE.

r003.rationale: It recommends expanding as capability grows, but does not state that killer applications at successive stages sustain the product’s growth.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to separate the product’s form from the problems it solves. A general-purpose product can give users one place to bring many different tasks, but that doesn’t mean you should build every use case at once. You still need to pick concrete problems and solve them well.

For something like Midas, I would start with a few applications where we can understand what success looks like and get feedback from users. Can it finish the task? How much intervention does it need? Would someone come back and use it again? Those questions are much easier to answer than whether a product is generally useful.

Then you look at what transfers across those applications. Maybe several tasks need the same ability to gather information, use tools, or check a result. Improving those shared capabilities gives you a path toward something more general. So I’d keep the overall product open-ended, while being quite focused about what we make reliable at each stage.

r001.rationale: The response says the product can remain open-ended while focusing on a few concrete applications and making them reliable at each stage.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the potential application ceiling of a general-purpose product form with a domain-specific form such as an IDE.

r003.rationale: It describes focused applications as a path toward broader capabilities, but does not state that killer applications at successive stages sustain the product’s growth.
